title: Honest placebo
hookLine: pills openly labeled as placebo still helped some patients (Kaptchuk et al., 2010)

cards: A patient sits across from a clinician and is handed a bottle of pills. The clinician explains, plainly, that there's no medicine in them. They're placebo pills, inert, like sugar pills.
Take them twice a day anyway. No trick, nothing hidden. It sounds like the setup for a joke.
It was a real study. And the patients who took the honest placebo reported feeling better than the patients who got no pills at all. So what on earth was in that bottle?

teach.b: First, the study. Ted Kaptchuk and colleagues worked with people who had irritable bowel syndrome.
One group was given pills openly labeled placebo and told the truth: no active ingredient, but placebos can sometimes help. The other group got no pills, with the same warm attention from the staff.
The placebo group reported more relief. Second, the honest size.
It was a small study, of one condition, and the symptoms were reported by the patients themselves. So last week's question applies: was it repeated? A finding to hold with interest, not a cure.
Third, what might be going on.
The researchers point to the ritual around the pill: the bottle, the routine, the clear explanation, being taken seriously by someone who cares.

The pill carried no medicine, but the ritual around it may have carried something. Fourth, the word itself. In the Latin Bible, a psalm line begins with that very word: "Placebo Domino in regione vivorum."
The Douay-Rheims translation renders it: "I will please the Lord in the land of the living."
To be clear, none of this says anything about whether prayer or worship is real. Believers understand their own rituals in their own terms, and tomorrow takes up prayer directly.
Today is smaller: a routine, done with care, seems to do something for the person doing it.

how: Researchers study "open-label" placebos by telling patients plainly that the pills contain no medicine; people, religious or not, also keep small daily rituals, such as lighting a candle or making tea, to mark a beginning.

o: pills openly labeled as empty that still helped some patients
a fake treatment that researchers proved works for every illness
a sugar pill given secretly, so patients think it's real medicine

p: no pills, the same warm attention

s: the patients were tricked into thinking the pills were medicine
they were told plainly that the pills had no active ingredient.
in the Latin Bible, a psalm line begins with the word placebo
the Douay-Rheims renders it "I will please the Lord in the land of the living."
the study shows that prayer is just a placebo
it says nothing about prayer or worship. it was a small study of one condition.

games.q: you're in the study. the clinician hands you a bottle and says the pills contain no medicine. what do you do?
o: take them twice a day, as asked.
take them, but secretly expect nothing.
games.why: the patients took them as asked, knowing what they were, and the placebo group reported more relief than the no-pill group.

practice: Bring to mind one small ritual in your day, filling the kettle, lighting a candle, washing your face, the bell that starts this sit, and replay it slowly, step by step.
Notice what your body does as it begins: does the breath change, do the shoulders drop? Don't decide what it means; just watch, and if you pray, notice what your own way of beginning prayer does too.

wordCard.voice: Honest placebo. Pills openly labeled as containing no medicine still helped some patients, perhaps through the ritual of care around them. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, from the Latin Bible's psalm line "Placebo Domino": I will please. In English, said pluh-SEE-boh.

carryVoice: Your line: ritual helps. The bottle was empty; the care around it wasn't. Tomorrow, prayer goes to the lab.

sources.ref: Kaptchuk et al., "Placebos without deception: a randomized controlled trial in irritable bowel syndrome" (PLoS ONE, 2010)

sources.q: I will please the Lord in the land of the living.
